newsitem.title: USA: Swiss bank guard now a U.S. resident - D'Amato.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank guard now a U.S. resident - D'Amato.

text.p: A Swiss bank guard who said he saved Holocaust-era bank files from the shredder has been granted permanent residency status in the United States, Sen. Alfonse D'Amato said on Wednesday.
Christoph Meili, his wife and two young children became permanent U.S. residents on Tuesday after President Bill Clinton signed a bill tailored for them, D'Amato said.

Meili found the files in January while a guard at the Union Bank of Switzerland. He has since been fired by the bank's security firm and said at a news conference with D'Amato that he is considering job offers in the United States.

D'Amato, a New York Republican, called on Switzerland and UBS to apologise to Meili and that his lost salary be reimbursed. D'Amato also said penalties would be considered if an apology was not forthcoming.
"If you do not act, we will be forced to act and that could take the form of severe penalties," D'Amato said in a letter to Swiss President Arnold Koller.

D'Amato said those penalties could include an inquiry into whether Switzerland had violated two accords between the Allied powers of the Second World War and Switzerland with regard to turning over all German accounts from its banks.

According to D'Amato, other possible penalties include: a Federal Reserve Board review to determine whether UBS's authority to operate in the United States should be terminated or restricted; revocation of a provision that lets UBS engage in securities underwriting and other non-bank activities in the United States; and a request that New York state review whether UBS's license to operate in New York be suspended or revoked.
Earlier on Wednesday in Zurich, Swiss prosecutors and UBS rejected Meili's claims that the files he saved were more extensive than UBS had disclosed.

UBS, Switzerland's biggest bank, maintains the documents were records of 31 properties held by a subsidiary bank in Germany, including three whose previous owners might have been Jewish. Meili has said the documents listed 45 properties, all of which he said were Jewish-owned.
